lessons.title: Costing and Pricing Seedlings
lessons.body:
To make a profit from your nursery, you must know exactly how much it costs to produce one seedling. Start by listing all your costs for a batch of 1,000 seedlings. This includes: seeds (e.g., tomato seeds at $20 per 10g), potting soil (e.g., 10 bags of compost at $5 each), polythene tubes (1,000 tubes at $0.02 each), water (e.g., $10 per month), labour (e.g., 2 workers for 5 days at $5 per day), and transport to market ($15). Add these up: $20 + $50 + $20 + $10 + $50 + $15 = $165. That is your total cost. Now divide by 1,000 seedlings to get the cost per seedling: $0.165. But you also need to account for lossesâmaybe 10% of seedlings die or are unsellable. So your effective cost per sellable seedling is $0.165 / 0.9 = $0.183. 

Next, decide on your selling price. You want a profit margin of at least 30-50%. If your cost is $0.183, a 50% markup gives a price of $0.275, round to $0.30 per seedling. For grafted or potted plants, costs are higherâgrafting may add $0.50 per plant for labour and rootstock, so price accordingly. Check local market prices: in many African towns, a tomato seedling sells for $0.20-$0.50, while a grafted mango seedling can sell for $2-$5. 

Remember to review your costs regularly. Seed and input prices change with seasons and inflation. Keep a simple notebook or use a mobile app like Excel or a free farm records app to track expenses. If you sell in bulk to retailers, offer a discount (e.g., 10% off for orders over 500 seedlings) but ensure you still cover costs. 

Always calculate your break-even point: total costs divided by selling price per seedling. For example, $165 / $0.30 = 550 seedlings. You must sell at least 550 to cover costs; every seedling after that is profit. This simple math keeps your nursery in business.

lessons.title: Record Keeping and Inventory Management
lessons.body:
Good records are the backbone of a profitable nursery. Without them, you won't know if you are making money or losing it. Start with a simple cash book: a notebook with columns for date, description, money in, money out, and balance. Record every sale, even a single seedling sold for $0.50. Also record every expense: seeds, tubes, water bills, labour, transport. At the end of each week, total your income and expenses to see your profit or loss. 

For inventory, you need to track how many seedlings you have at each stage. Use a whiteboard or a spreadsheet to list: seed sown, germinated, pricked out, ready for sale, and sold. For example, if you sow 1,000 tomato seeds, note the date. After 7 days, count how many germinated. After 21 days, count how many are ready. This helps you plan sales and avoid overproduction. 

Also track your inputs: bags of soil, tubes, seeds, and fertiliser. Keep a minimum stock levelâsay, when you have only 200 tubes left, order more. This prevents last-minute shortages. Use a simple inventory sheet or a mobile app like 'Farm Manager' or 'Excel'. 

At the end of each month, do a physical count of all seedlings and compare with your records. If there is a difference, investigate: theft, disease, or miscounting. Accurate records also help you get loans or grantsâbanks want to see your books. 

Finally, keep records for at least 5 years. They help you spot trends: which crops sell best, which months are slow, and which customers pay on time. This data is gold for planning your next season.

lessons.title: Marketing Strategies for Local Sales
lessons.body:
Marketing your seedlings doesn't require a big budgetâjust creativity and consistency. Start by identifying your local market: farmers, gardeners, schools, churches, and retailers. Visit them in person. Dress neatly, carry a sample of your best seedlings, and explain why your plants are healthy and high-yielding. For example, tell a tomato farmer: 'These are hybrid Anna F1, they resist wilt and give 30% more yield.' 

Use word-of-mouth: give a free seedling to a respected farmer in the village. When they succeed, they will tell others. Offer a 'refer a friend' discount: if a customer brings a new buyer, give them 10% off their next purchase. 

Create simple flyers or posters using a phone app like Canva, and print at a local shop. Include your phone number, location, and prices. Put them at agro-dealers, markets, and community notice boards. 

Leverage WhatsApp and Facebook. Create a WhatsApp group for your customers. Post photos of your seedlings weekly, share tips on planting, and announce special offers. For example: 'Buy 100 tomato seedlings, get 10 free this week only.' 

Attend local farmer field days or agricultural shows. Set up a small stall with healthy seedlings and a price list. Collect phone numbers of interested farmers. 

Partner with agro-vets: they sell seeds and fertiliser, so let them display your seedlings on commission (e.g., 20% of sales). This gives you access to their customers. 

Finally, always deliver on time and ensure quality. A bad batch ruins your reputation. Consistent quality and friendly service will make you the go-to nursery in your area.

lessons.title: Selling to Farmers, Gardeners, and Retailers
lessons.body:
Different customers have different needs, so tailor your sales approach. Farmers buy in bulkâthey need hundreds or thousands of seedlings. They care about price, disease resistance, and yield. Offer volume discounts: e.g., $0.25 per seedling for 100-499, $0.22 for 500-999, $0.20 for 1,000+. Provide technical advice: give a free planting guide with each bulk order. Farmers also want deliveryâif you can deliver to their farm for a small fee, you gain an edge. 

Gardeners buy smaller quantitiesâ10 to 50 seedlingsâand often want variety: vegetables, herbs, flowers. They are willing to pay a premium for healthy, potted plants. Sell them in attractive pots or trays. Offer a 'garden starter kit' with 10 different seedlings for $5. Gardeners also appreciate advice on care. 

Retailers (agro-shops, supermarkets) buy in bulk but expect a wholesale price. They need a steady supply and attractive packaging. Offer them a 20-30% discount off retail price, and provide branded labels or tags. For example, a retailer might buy 500 seedlings at $0.18 each and sell at $0.30. Build a contract: agree on weekly or monthly deliveries. 

For all customers, keep a customer register with names, phone numbers, and purchase history. Follow up after a week to ask how the seedlings are performing. This builds loyalty. 

Payment: accept cash, mobile money (M-Pesa, Airtel Money), or bank transfer. For large orders, ask for a 50% deposit. Always issue a receipt. 

Remember, farmers talk to each other. A satisfied farmer will refer you to others. So treat every customer like your best customer.

lessons.title: Value Addition: Grafted and Potted Plants
lessons.body:
Value addition means turning a basic seedling into a premium product that sells for more. Two proven methods are grafting and potting. Grafting involves joining a scion (top part) from a desired variety onto a rootstock that has strong roots or disease resistance. For example, graft a tasty mango variety onto a hardy local rootstock. Grafted plants sell for 3-5 times more than ordinary seedlings: a regular mango seedling might sell for $1, but a grafted one can fetch $3-$5. 

To graft, you need: a sharp knife, grafting tape, and rootstock seedlings (e.g., 6-month-old mango or avocado). The best time is during the rainy season when sap is flowing. Techniques include cleft grafting and whip grafting. Practice on a few plants first. After grafting, keep the plants in a shaded nursery for 2-3 weeks. 

Potted plants: instead of selling bare-root seedlings, grow them in attractive pots or polybags. Use a good potting mix (soil, compost, sand in 3:2:1 ratio). Potted plants are ready for sale when they are 30-50 cm tall. They appeal to urban gardeners and landscapers. A potted tomato plant might sell for $2 instead of $0.30 for a bare seedling. 

Other value additions: sell seedlings in trays (e.g., 50-cell trays) for easy transplanting. Offer 'ready-to-plant' kits with a seedling, a pot, and a small bag of fertiliser. 

Marketing these premium products: target hotels, offices, and wealthy homeowners. Use social media to show beautiful potted plants. Price them based on the extra cost: a grafted plant costs you an extra $0.50 in labour and materials, so price it at least $1.50 above a regular seedling. 

Value addition increases your income and sets you apart from competitors who only sell ordinary seedlings.

lessons.title: Customer Service and Repeat Business
lessons.body:
Good customer service is what turns a one-time buyer into a loyal customer. Start with a friendly greeting and a clean, organised nursery. When a customer arrives, ask what they want to grow and offer advice. For example, if they want tomatoes, ask if they have had disease problems before, and recommend a resistant variety. 

Be honest about your products. If a seedling is not the best for their area, say so and suggest an alternative. This builds trust. Always give a receipt and a planting guide. Follow up after a week with a phone call or WhatsApp message: 'How are your seedlings doing? Need any tips?' This simple act makes customers feel valued. 

Handle complaints quickly. If a customer says seedlings died, ask questions: did they water properly? Was there too much sun? If the fault is yours (e.g., diseased seedlings), replace them free of charge. A refund or replacement costs less than a bad reputation. 

Offer a loyalty programme: after 5 purchases, give a 10% discount or a free seedling. Keep a record of customer purchases in a notebook or phone. Send SMS reminders when new stock arrives or when it's planting season. 

Encourage repeat business by offering a 'season pass': pay a fixed amount and get a certain number of seedlings each month. Or offer a subscription for vegetable gardeners: 10 seedlings delivered monthly for 6 months. 

Finally, always thank your customers and ask for feedback. Use their suggestions to improve. A customer who feels heard will come back and bring friends. In the nursery business, your reputation is your most valuable asset.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Nursery Business and Marketing

This practical reference consolidates the core commercial skills needed to turn a seedling nursery from a subsistence activity into a viable agribusiness. It is written for smallholder and emerging commercial nursery operators across sub-Saharan Africa, where demand for quality planting material is rising rapidly â driven by reforestation programmes, horticulture expansion, and government input subsidy schemes. The lessons covered here â costing and pricing, record keeping, marketing, selling to different customer segments, value addition, and customer service â are the difference between a nursery that survives one season and one that trades for a decade.

Throughout, the focus is on decisions you can act on this week: how to set a price that covers your costs and still wins the sale, how to keep records that a bank will accept, and how to build a customer base that returns every planting season.

Costing and Pricing Seedlings

Most nursery failures in Africa are pricing failures, not production failures. A seedling sold below its full cost of production destroys working capital, even when sales volumes look healthy. You must first know your cost per seedling, then add a margin.

Separate your costs into fixed costs (land rent, nursery shed, tools, water infrastructure, licences) and variable costs (seed, potting media, polythene tubes, labour, water, transport). Divide total fixed costs by the number of seedlings you realistically sell in a season to get the fixed cost per seedling. Add variable cost per seedling. That is your break-even price.

Table 1: Sample cost build-up for 1,000 grafted mango seedlings (Kenya, indicative)
Cost itemTotal (KSh)Per seedling (KSh)
Rootstock seed & scion material6,0006.00
Potting media & polythene tubes9,0009.00
Labour (grafting, watering, weeding)18,00018.00
Water & nursery inputs4,0004.00
Fixed costs (shade, rent, tools) apportioned8,0008.00
Total cost45,00045.00
Target margin (40%)18,00018.00
Recommended selling price63,00063.00

Source: Adapted from KALRO Horticultural Nursery Costing Guidelines and AgriProFocus East Africa nursery enterprise budgets. Figures are illustrative only â replace with your own records.

Pricing rules that work: price grafted and certified seedlings at a premium (they carry higher input costs and buyer confidence); offer tiered pricing â full price for single units, 5â10% discount for 50+, 15% for 500+; never discount below break-even to win a bulk order unless the buyer covers transport and pays upfront.

Record Keeping and Inventory Management

Records are not paperwork for its own sake â they are the evidence that unlocks credit, contracts, and better decisions. Keep four registers: a cash book (every shilling in and out, dated), a production log (sowing dates, germination rates, losses), an inventory register (seed, media, pots, and seedling stock by species and age), and a sales ledger (buyer, quantity, price, payment status).

Table 2: Monthly seedling inventory and sales tracker (template)

Source: Template adapted from FAO Farm Records and Inventory Management for Smallholders and the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition (GAIN) smallholder business record templates.

Reconcile inventory weekly. If closing stock does not match physical count, investigate immediately â unexplained seedling losses are usually theft, water stress, or unrecorded sales, and all three destroy margin.

Marketing Strategies for Local Sales

Marketing in a nursery context is about visibility at the moment a farmer is deciding what to plant. The most effective channels in African contexts are:

  • Demonstration plots and field days â invite farmers to see grafted versus non-grafted performance side by side. This is the single highest-converting marketing activity.
  • Radio and local-language WhatsApp groups â low-cost, high-reach, especially for seasonal planting reminders.
  • Agro-dealer partnerships â place stock on consignment or wholesale terms with input shops farmers already visit.
  • Signage and road-front nursery display â a well-labelled, tidy nursery visible from a main road generates walk-in sales.
  • County agriculture officers and extension agents â they recommend suppliers; cultivate the relationship.

Selling to Farmers, Gardeners, and Retailers

Each segment buys differently and must be served differently. Farmers buy in bulk, are price-sensitive, and buy at the start of the rains â they need credit terms or mobile money convenience, and they need assurance on variety and yield. Gardeners buy small quantities at higher unit prices and care about plant health and appearance â packaging and advice matter more than price. Retailers (agro-dealers, supermarkets, landscapers) buy on wholesale terms, need reliable supply and consistent quality, and will return if you deliver on time.

Build a simple customer register: name, segment, contact, what they bought, and when they are likely to buy again. This single habit converts one-off buyers into repeat customers.

Value Addition: Grafted and Potted Plants

Grafting and decorative potting raise both price and customer perception of quality. A grafted avocado or mango can sell for two to five times the price of a seedling of unknown parentage because the buyer is purchasing guaranteed variety, earlier fruiting, and disease resistance. Potted ornamental and herb plants open a second market â urban households, hotels, and landscapers â that is less seasonal than farm sales.

Value addition requires investment: training in grafting technique, clean tools, grafting tape, and a shade structure for hardening. Treat this as a capital investment with a payback period you can calculate from the price premium.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Pesticides, Sterilisation and Grafting Tools

Nursery work involves real hazards. Always wear gloves, eye protection, and a mask when mixing or applying pesticides, fungicides, or soil sterilants â many products used in nurseries are toxic and can cause serious poisoning or long-term health damage. Never mix chemicals in food containers, never store them near seed or media, and always follow the label and the manufacturer's re-entry interval. Sterilise grafting knives and secateurs between plants with methylated spirit or a 10% bleach solution to prevent spreading disease. Keep sharp tools sheathed and out of reach of children. Store all agrochemicals in a locked cabinet, and keep the nearest poison control or clinic number posted on the nursery wall. In case of suspected poisoning, seek medical help immediately and take the product label with you.

Customer Service and Repeat Business

Repeat business is the cheapest sale you will ever make. A farmer who trusts you returns every season and refers neighbours. Deliver on three promises: quality (healthy, true-to-variety seedlings), reliability (the quantity and species you promised, on the date promised), and advice (planting guidance, spacing, aftercare). Follow up two to four weeks after a sale with a phone call or WhatsApp message asking how the plants are performing. This single act builds loyalty that no advertisement can buy.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Calculate cost per seedling (fixed + variable) before setting any price.
  • â Set a target margin of at least 30â40% above full cost.
  • â Keep a daily cash book and a weekly inventory reconciliation.
  • â Maintain a customer register with contact details and purchase history.
  • â Run at least one demonstration plot or field day per season.
  • â Offer tiered pricing for bulk buyers without breaching break-even.
  • â Invest in grafting and potting only after calculating the price premium and payback.
  • â Follow up with every buyer within one month of sale.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Nursery Manual for Forest Tree Species (free PDF)
  • CIFOR-ICRAF â Tree Nursery and Agroforestry Publications (free)
  • KALRO â Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organisation (crop and nursery guides)
  • AgriFin â Smallholder Agribusiness and Finance Resources (free)
  • GAIN â Smallholder Business and Record-Keeping Tools (free)

Prepared as a practical reference for the RISE AFRICA skills course Seedling Nursery for Farmers â Module: Nursery Business and Marketing. Figures are indicative and must be replaced with locally verified costs and prices.

quiz.q: What is the first step in costing seedlings?
options: C) Count the number of seedlings
quiz.explanation: You must know your costs before you can set a price.

quiz.q: If total cost for 1,000 seedlings is $165 and 10% are lost, what is the cost per sellable seedling?
quiz.explanation: Divide total cost by 900 sellable seedlings: $165/900 = $0.183.

quiz.q: What profit margin is recommended for seedling pricing?
quiz.explanation: A 30-50% markup covers costs and provides reasonable profit.

quiz.q: What is the break-even point if total costs are $165 and selling price is $0.30 per seedling?
quiz.explanation: $165 / $0.30 = 550 seedlings to cover costs.

quiz.q: Why should you review costs regularly?
quiz.explanation: Seed, labour, and transport costs fluctuate, affecting your profit.

quiz.q: What is a simple tool for record keeping?
quiz.explanation: A cash book tracks money in and out easily.

quiz.q: How often should you do a physical count of seedlings?
quiz.explanation: Monthly counts help reconcile records and detect losses.

quiz.q: What should you track in inventory?
options: B) Seeds, tubes, and seedlings at each stage
quiz.explanation: Tracking inputs and plant stages prevents shortages and overproduction.

quiz.q: Why keep records for at least 5 years?
quiz.explanation: Long-term records help with loans, trends, and tax compliance.

quiz.q: What is a minimum stock level?
options: A) The most you can store
B) The least you should have before reordering
quiz.explanation: It triggers reordering to avoid running out.

quiz.q: Which is a low-cost marketing strategy?
quiz.explanation: Word-of-mouth is free and effective in local communities.

quiz.q: What should a flyer include?
options: A) Your phone number and prices
quiz.explanation: Customers need contact details and prices to buy.

quiz.q: How can you use WhatsApp for marketing?
quiz.explanation: WhatsApp groups allow you to share updates and promotions.

quiz.q: What is a 'refer a friend' discount?
options: A) A discount for new customers
B) A reward for bringing new buyers
quiz.explanation: It encourages existing customers to refer others.

quiz.q: Why partner with agro-vets?
quiz.explanation: Agro-vets already have farmer customers who may buy seedlings.

quiz.q: What do farmers buying in bulk care about most?
quiz.explanation: Farmers focus on cost-effectiveness and productivity.

quiz.q: What is a volume discount?
quiz.explanation: Encourages larger purchases by reducing unit price.

quiz.q: What do gardeners often want?
quiz.explanation: Gardeners buy small quantities and prefer diverse, attractive plants.

quiz.q: What should you ask for on large orders?
quiz.explanation: A deposit reduces risk of non-payment.

quiz.q: Why keep a customer register?
options: A) To track purchases and follow up
quiz.explanation: It helps build relationships and repeat business.

quiz.q: What is grafting?
options: A) Joining a scion to a rootstock
quiz.explanation: Grafting combines desired variety with hardy roots.

quiz.q: How much more can a grafted mango seedling sell for?
quiz.explanation: Grafted plants command a premium due to their benefits.

quiz.q: What is needed for grafting?
quiz.explanation: A clean cut and secure wrapping are essential.

quiz.q: What is a good potting mix ratio?
quiz.explanation: This mix provides drainage and nutrients.

quiz.q: Why are potted plants more valuable?
options: A) They are ready to plant and attractive
quiz.explanation: Convenience and aesthetics justify higher prices.

quiz.q: What is a value-added product?
quiz.explanation: Value addition increases price and differentiation.

quiz.q: Why follow up with customers after a sale?
options: A) To ask for more money
B) To show care and offer help
C) To sell them new seeds
quiz.explanation: Follow-up builds loyalty and trust.

quiz.q: What should you do if a customer complains about dead seedlings?
options: C) Replace or refund if your fault
quiz.explanation: Resolving complaints fairly retains customers.

quiz.q: What is a loyalty programme?
options: A) A discount for frequent buyers
B) A free gift for everyone
quiz.explanation: Rewards repeat customers and encourages more purchases.

quiz.q: Why is customer service important for repeat business?
options: B) It builds reputation and trust
quiz.explanation: Good service makes customers return and refer others.
